paras: The lynching of Bob Haggard was the hanging of a Black man by a mob in Kentucky in mid-July 1895, after he was accused of assaulting a young woman named Miss Elkin. Within days a wire report datelined Ford, Ky., said he had been innocent and that the story of the crime was false, and newspapers across the country ran the item under headlines such as "Lynched an Innocent Man." Kentucky papers placed the lynching at Winchester, and no report of an arrest was found.

Haggard, whose surname some Kentucky papers printed as Hazzard, was charged with having "outraged" Miss Elkin, also spelled Elkins. According to one version of the wire report, Haggard "admitted that he had been intimate with the girl, but said he had never assaulted her." The Louisville Courier-Journal later gave the mob's motive as "fear that courts would not inflict proper punishment for crime of assault."

The fullest account of the killing came from the Cannelton Enquirer, reprinted in the Hartford Republican, which said "a mob of blue bloods" dragged Haggard from jail at Winchester and hanged him from a bridge. By that account he was let down and slowly strangled, and fifteen minutes passed before his body stopped showing signs of life. The Courier-Journal dated the hanging July 16, while Judge Albion W. Tourgee's list of the month's mob murders gave July 14.

Around July 26 it was reported that Haggard had been innocent and that the account of the crime had been "proven to be utterly false." The Hickman Courier described this more cautiously as "rumors at Winchester" of his innocence. The Cannelton Enquirer wrote that "there was no assault committed" and that, according to the daily press, the mob's leaders had said they were sorry.

The Courier-Journal's list of Kentucky killings since July 1 recorded "no attempt at arrest, though names of many of the mob known." No report of an inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The story reached most readers through a short wire item datelined Ford, Ky., July 27 to 29, which ran in early August in papers from Texas and Mississippi to Minnesota, Wisconsin, North Dakota, Michigan and Vermont. Its headlines stressed the error rather than the killing ("Lynched an Innocent Man," "The Wrong Man"), though the Greenville Times led with "NEGRO LYNCHED." The item called Haggard "the negro" and attributed the lynching to "a few hot-headed men who did not take time to inquire whether Haggard was guilty or not," and weekly digests cut it to a single sentence.

Kentucky papers named Winchester instead of Ford and treated the case in different registers. The Cannelton Enquirer piece, reprinted by the Hartford Republican on August 16 under "Hung an Innocent Man," mocked the mob's regret and closed, "Winchester is in Kentucky, gentlemen, and we have never seen the place." The Courier-Journal, by contrast, listed the hanging in a single line among the state's killings.

The case also entered national tallies of mob violence. On August 4 the Indianapolis Journal editorialized that two Black men lynched in the South within two weeks had been proved innocent, without naming them. On August 31 the New York Sun printed a letter signed T. Thomas Fortune that reproduced Tourgee's July list, with Haggard's entry, as "sufficient to shock the moral sense of Christian mankind." No coverage of the lynching in the Black press was found for August and September 1895.

The wire placed the lynching at Ford, while the Hickman Courier, the Cannelton Enquirer, the Courier-Journal and Tourgee's list all placed it at Winchester. The wire also described the killers as "a few hot-headed men," whereas the Kentucky accounts described a mob whose members were largely known.

reader.title: Lynching of Bob Haggard
bases: A mob or group of men hanged Bob Haggard, a Black man accused of assaulting a girl, after taking him from jail (A4, A17, A18).

Haggard was hanged by 'a mob' that dragged him from jail, with no lawful authority, over an accusation of assault (A17, A18); the wire calls it the work of 'a few hot-headed men' (A4), and the Courier-Journal says the mob acted from fear the courts would not punish the crime (A18).

The Ford-datelined wire (A1, A4, A12), the Hickman Courier's Kentucky news (A6), the Cannelton Enquirer piece reprinted in Hartford (A17), the Courier-Journal's list (A18) and Tourgee's list (A19) all report that Haggard (or Hazzard) was lynched, though they differ on date and place.

accounts.label: Wire report (Ford, Ky.)
accounts.gist: Haggard, lynched at Ford 'last week' on a charge of outraging Miss Elkin, was found innocent; the story of the deed was false, and 'a few hot-headed men' had not inquired into his guilt.

accounts.label: Cannelton Enquirer (reprinted in Hartford Republican)
accounts.gist: A mob took Haggard from jail at Winchester and hanged him from a bridge, slowly strangling him; no assault had been committed and the leaders said they were sorry.

accounts.label: Courier-Journal list
accounts.gist: Robert Hazzard was hanged by a mob at Winchester on July 16 out of fear the courts would not punish the alleged assault; no arrest was attempted though many of the mob were known.

accounts.label: Tourgee's list (letter to the Sun)
accounts.gist: Bob Haggard, colored, hanged at Winchester, Ky., July 14.

framing.detail: Papers in Texas, Minnesota, Wisconsin, North Dakota, Vermont, Michigan and Mississippi ran the Ford item under 'Lynched an Innocent Man', 'The Wrong Man' or 'NEGRO LYNCHED', calling Haggard 'the negro' and blaming 'a few hot-headed men'.
The Hickman Courier reported only 'rumors at Winchester' of his innocence in a column of state news.
The Cannelton Enquirer, reprinted in Hartford, called it 'another case of "I told you so"', blamed 'a mob of blue bloods' and mocked the leaders' regret.
The Courier-Journal listed it flatly among Kentucky killings, noting no arrest was attempted.
Fortune's letter to the Sun cited Tourgee's July list, including Haggard, as 'sufficient to shock the moral sense of Christian mankind'.

conflicts.note: Ford appears only as the wire dateline ('lynched here'); every Kentucky source and Tourgee's list name Winchester, and the Courier-Journal list is the most specific local account.
The Courier-Journal is the Kentucky source with a dated entry; Tourgee's national list gives two days earlier.
Spelling variants of one victim; same accusation and place.
